1.0.0.en: 1 In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying, 2 “The LORD hath been sore displeased with your fathers. 3 Therefore say thou unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. 4 Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings: but they did not hear, nor hearken unto me, saith the LORD. 5 Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever? 6 But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers? and they returned and said, Like as the LORD of hosts thought to do unto us, according to our ways, and according to our doings, so hath he dealt with us.”

1.0.1.en: The prophet specified the date of his prophecy as the eighth month in the second year of Darius (520 B.C.), saying: “In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying” [1]. Here the prophet mentions his own name and the names of his father and his grandfather, perhaps mentioning his grandfather’s name because it was he who raised him after his father’s death, and because he was well known among those returning from the captivity (Neh 12:1, 4, 7).

1.1.0.en: The Lord’s call to them was: “The LORD hath been sore displeased with your fathers… Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts” [2-3]. We note here:

1.1.1.en: First: in this call He did not mention the details of their fathers’ past sins, for He did not want to wound their feelings after they had entered into the humiliation of captivity… Rather, even in urging them to repent, He wanted to support them, encourage them, and lift up their spirits.

1.1.2.en: Second: perhaps by their fathers He meant the generations before the captivity, which did not listen to the true prophets but followed the false prophets, so that the matter ended with the captivity of Israel and then of Judah. Or perhaps He meant those who had returned from the captivity about fifteen years earlier, who were negligent in building the temple and were absorbed in their earthly pleasures (Hag 1). These, in their zeal, had returned from the captivity to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, but since they did not return to the Lord with their hearts, the work stopped and they lost their spiritual life. Therefore the Lord affirms: “Turn ye unto me… and I will turn unto you.” Before the return to the place, He asks for the return of the heart to Him, while for His part He is ready, indeed longing, to return to us and build His spiritual temple within us. This is God’s continual call to us, and as St. Augustine says: [God in His long-suffering waits for the sinner, saying: “Turn ye unto me, and I will turn unto you.”] He also says: [By our complete return to God we find Him ready, as the prophet says: “We shall find Him ready as the morning” (Hos 6:3, Septuagint). God is not absent; He is present in every place, and it is we who lose Him by our deviation, for it is said: “He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not” (Jn 1:10). He was in the world and the world did not know Him, because the impurity of our eyes keeps us from seeing Him.] He also says: [God has forsaken you because you are the one who forsook. You are the one who fell away from Him, but as for Him, He does not fall away from you…].

1.1.3.en: Thus returning to God is not merely a change of place, that is, leaving Babylon and going to Jerusalem, but a change in the soul’s position toward God: instead of turning its back to Him with its evil deeds, it gives Him its face, drawing near to Him spiritually. As St. Didymus the Blind says: [This separation and this approach must not be understood as taking place in a particular place, but through the attitude and disposition of the spirit].

1.2.0.en: Third: He asks them to take warning from what happened to their fathers: “Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?” [5]. Perhaps He meant that He had forewarned their fathers through the prophets, but only for a time, and since they rejected the warning, they perished and lost the prophets. St. Didymus the Blind sees that He means by the prophets here the false prophets who deceived their fathers by saying to them: “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 11:8). They perished together with the false prophets who deceived them, and so the deceivers disappeared together with those who let themselves be deceived by their lies.

1.2.1.en: Fourth: in His call to return, God is called “the LORD of hosts,” His name being repeated three times in one passage [3]. On the one hand, the Lord comes forward to them as the Lord of hosts, to declare His responsibility for the work, so that they should not fear those who oppose, for He is able to accomplish the work through them if they submit to Him as spiritual soldiers to their commander. As for the expression “the LORD of hosts” three times at His call to repentance, it is an affirmation of the work of the Holy Trinity in their lives, for man cannot return to God unless he experiences the self-giving love of the Father, the grace of the Son through the Cross, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, the giver of forgiveness.

1.3.0.en: Fifth: this book affirms the important principle that God had already declared in the books of the prophets before the captivity, that what befalls them is chastening from the Lord, yet at the same time it is nothing but the natural fruit of sin… “According to our ways, and according to our doings, so hath he dealt with us” [6]. It is man himself who casts himself under chastening as the fruit of his deeds.

1.3.1.en: Sixth: if their fathers perished because of their clinging to evil, then whoever clings to vanity becomes vain; the remedy is to cling to the truth that he may live eternally. Thus God presents His word, that is, the truth, that we may cling to it and not die… “But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers?” [6]. As Isaiah says: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

1.4.0.en: 7 Upon the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Sebat, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying, 8 I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white. 9 Then said I, O my lord, what are these? And the angel that talked with me said unto me, I will shew thee what these be. 10 And the man that stood among the myrtle trees answered and said, These are they whom the LORD hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth. 11 And they answered the angel of the LORD that stood among the myrtle trees, and said, We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest.

1.5.0.en: Three months after the beginning of his prophecy came the month of Shebat, in which the trees put forth their shoots and the sweet fragrance of the myrtle tree spreads. Perhaps the prophet used to spend the whole day in a valley near him, falling on his knees under the shade of the myrtle trees, his tears never drying, crying out: “O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years?” [12]. In the midst of his weeping he turned his heart toward the temple which had become a ruin, and toward the people who had come about fifteen years earlier to build the temple, but each one was absorbed in his own work and personal interests. The prophet, as a priest, was groaning, longing for the return of the temple with its spiritual rites, which he had not practiced from his birth until that moment. Therefore at night God granted him this vision: “I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white. Then said I, O my lord, what are these? And the angel that talked with me said unto me, I will shew thee what these be. And the man that stood among the myrtle trees answered and said, These are they whom the LORD hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth. And they answered the angel of the LORD that stood among the myrtle trees, and said, We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest” [8-11].

1.5.1.en: By this vision God declares His saving plans and His care for His spiritual house. God also gave him an angel to speak with him, who accompanied him in all the visions, entering into dialogue with him and explaining to him what was obscure to him. It is as though the Lord wanted to affirm heaven’s support for him and the ministry of the angels to men (Heb 1:14).

1.5.2.en: Now, who is this man riding on a red horse, standing among the myrtle trees that were in the shade, who is called “the angel of the LORD”?

1.5.3.en: The expression “the angel of the LORD” most often refers to God Himself when He appears as an angel or a messenger for the sake of man, for the word “angel” means “messenger.” It is stated in the Babylonian Talmud: “This man is none other than the Holy One, blessed be He, for it is said: ‘The LORD is a man of war.’” St. Didymus the Blind says: [The one riding on a red horse is the Lord the Savior incarnate, and the red horse is the body that He put on. The prophet saw Him “standing among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom,” that is, among the shaded mountains. The mountains are the two Testaments. They are for me fertile mountains, shaded because of the wealth of thoughts and the abundance of the texts of Scripture about the Incarnate One].”

1.5.4.en: We can say that the prophet saw this vision “by night” [8], that is, during the Old Testament, when the Lord Christ, the Sun of Righteousness who turned the night of the world into day, had not yet appeared. He saw Him through the prophecies, therefore he saw Him in the shade, His coming not yet having been fulfilled. He saw Him as a man riding upon a red horse, since He became incarnate and became man, coming forward to us with His divine work through the Cross, where the blood was shed, as Isaiah said: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments… Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat? I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” (Isa 63:1-3).

1.5.5.en: The prophet saw behind the Lord Christ red, speckled, and white horses, of whom the Lord said: “These are they whom the LORD hath sent to walk to and fro through the earth” [10]. With the coming of the Lord Christ to us for salvation, heaven was opened and the heavenly ones turned to the service of man on behalf of the heavenly Bridegroom, and became like those who walk to and fro through the earth to minister to those who shall be heirs of salvation (Heb 1:14).

1.5.6.en: Perhaps those whom the Lord sent to walk to and fro through the earth are the men of the Old Testament who prepared the earth to receive the Incarnate Word through their teachings and prophecies; these preceded Him on the way, yet they remain behind Him as their Lord and Savior. As for their answer: “We have walked to and fro through the earth, and, behold, all the earth sitteth still, and is at rest” [11], it points to the preparation of the earth to receive the Messiah the Savior, for the way had been prepared and the time was suitable for His coming down.

1.5.7.en: If the rider on the red horse symbolizes the Incarnate Word of God, then these horses of different colors perhaps signify the divine works, as though the prophet is declaring to the Jewish people at that time that God had offered various works and prepared for them by every means an atmosphere of calm: the whole earth is still and at rest, there is no one to oppose and no one to devise plots against them, so they must hasten to build the house of the Lord. In the same sense we say that the prophet declares that the Lord Christ has sent us His red, speckled, and white horses, offering us every heavenly gift and divine bestowal in order to make our earth, that is, our body, still and calm, not resisting the Spirit but working with Him for the glory of God. It is a time for work, in which it is fitting for us to consecrate all our spiritual and bodily energies to the spiritual building of our heavenly Jerusalem.

1.5.8.en: This is the first vision that lifted Zechariah out of his daily tears in the valley of the myrtle trees under the shade, to bring him into the valley of the work of God declared through the Incarnation and the crucifixion! By this Zechariah was taken from the distress of his soul to true peace and rest, therefore he said: “All the earth sitteth still, and is at rest.”

1.5.9.en: Let us not understand the earth’s being at rest and still in the sense of idleness and slackness, but in the sense of enjoying the surpassing peace of God, as St. Didymus the Blind says: [The rational soul carries an energy that moves it in continual activity, but since it works for the sake of the good, it remains calm and at rest without disturbance, enjoying the inner peace that the fear of God brings… As it is written: “But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil” (Prov 1:33)].

1.5.10.en: In Christ Jesus our Lord our souls and also our bodies, that is, our inner heavens and our earth, become at rest, being sanctified by Him and rejoicing, though bearing His cross and entering with Him into His tomb.

1.6.s.en: 3. The Lord’s jealousy for His house:

1.6.0.en: 12 Then the angel of the LORD answered and said, O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years? 13 And the LORD answered the angel that talked with me with good words and comfortable words. 14 So the angel that communed with me said unto me, Cry thou, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy. 15 And I am very sore displeased with the heathen that are at ease: for I was but a little displeased, and they helped forward the affliction. 16 Therefore thus saith the LORD; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem. 17 Cry yet, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; My cities through prosperity shall yet be spread abroad; and the LORD shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem.

1.7.0.en: If the prophet Zechariah spent years contemplating the ruin of the temple with tears that never dried, asking God for the rebuilding of the temple, then our Lord Jesus Christ is the only propitiatory Intercessor who cries out with His precious blood for the raising up of His sanctuaries in humanity, for it is said: “Then the angel of the LORD answered and said, O LORD of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, against which thou hast had indignation these threescore and ten years?” Humanity fell under the captivity of the enemy of good for years of such measure, and no one could intercede for it except the One who offered His blood as an atonement for our sins, bringing divine mercy by paying the debt of divine justice on the Cross. His intercession was not mere words but a work full of love and effective, by which He was able to remove the divine wrath from those who believe in Him and bring them into God’s mercies, that His holy heavenly temple might be raised up in them. This is the good words and comfortable words which the angel who accompanied him declared [13].

1.8.0.en: By the Cross the Lord says: “I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy. And I am very sore displeased with the heathen that are at ease: for I was but a little displeased, and they helped forward the affliction. Therefore thus saith the LORD; I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts, and a line shall be stretched forth upon Jerusalem. Cry yet, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; My cities through prosperity shall yet be spread abroad; and the LORD shall yet comfort Zion, and shall yet choose Jerusalem” [14-17]. From the historical side this was fulfilled literally: after the captivity of Judah for seventy years God declared His jealousy for His city and His people, when the nations were at ease, thinking that they had completely humbled the people of God, laid waste the Promised Land, and destroyed the holy temple; some of them took the main part, like the Babylonians, and others shared in the work, like the Edomites, or by gloating… But while they were at ease the Lord returned to Jerusalem to raise up His house anew and to permit the stretching forth of the line (the instrument for measuring the wall), not for demolition as at the time of the captivity because of the crookedness of the walls, but for the raising of buildings and rebuilding; and thus He pours out good upon His people and declares His love and care for them.

1.8.1.en: This was fulfilled literally in the sixth century B.C., but it was fulfilled in a fuller way and with a deeper meaning in the Messianic age, when the Lord ascended His Cross stretching out His hands with blessing to humanity, shattering the captivity of the devil and granting true good to those who believe in Him, as St. Paul says: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Rom 8:32). He returned to us with His mercies to raise up His temple in us, saying: “The kingdom of God is within you.” He stretched forth His hand with the line to build and increase our inner life, so that blessings and consolations overflow from the fruit of His Holy Spirit (Jn 15:26), revealing His choice of our inner Jerusalem as His bride.

1.8.2.en: What is this house that occupies the heart of God?

1.8.3.en: First: the Church which the Lord raises up as His bride, to which the Apostle pointed by his saying: “But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Tim 3:15).

1.8.4.en: Second: St. Didymus says: [This house is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose heart is a dwelling for Him, one with the divinity without mixing or separation, of which He said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up… But he spake of the temple of his body” (Jn 2:19, 21). This is the house announced by the book of Proverbs: “Wisdom hath builded her house” (Prov 9:1)].

1.8.5.en: Third: St. Didymus concludes his discourse on this house by saying: [We must also add that every believer is likewise a house built to be a temple of God. Scripture says: “Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” (1 Cor 3:16). The Savior Himself says plainly: “If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him” (Jn 14:23)].

1.9.s.en: 4. The vision of the four horns:

1.9.0.en: 18 Then lifted I up mine eyes, and saw, and behold four horns. 19 And I said unto the angel that talked with me, What be these? And he answered me, These are the horns which have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. 20 And the LORD shewed me four carpenters. 21 Then said I, What come these to do? And he spake, saying, These are the horns which have scattered Judah, so that no man did lift up his head: but these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah to scatter it.

1.10.0.en: According to the Hebrew canon, the second chapter of this book begins with this second vision, concerning the appearance of the four horns which scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem so that no man did lift up his head [21], and then the appearance of four craftsmen who rose up to spread terror and to cast out these horns of the Gentiles.

1.10.1.en: Perhaps the prophet Zechariah in his solitude was looking in every direction of the inhabited world, to see the nations as though they were striking Jerusalem with their horn without ceasing and without mercy. The Jews were familiar with the tending of sheep and knew the blows of the horns of horned beasts, how they kill the sheep and scatter them; therefore the psalmist says: “Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps 22:21). The prophet Daniel speaks of the horn that made war with the saints and prevailed against them until the Ancient of days came (Dan 7:21-22). Thus horns became a sign of power and authority, for the Lord says in Micah: “Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the LORD, and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth” (Mic 4:13).

1.10.2.en: In this vision of the four horns the following is to be noted:

1.10.3.en: First: some see in these four horns a reference to the kingdoms that humbled the people, namely the kingdom of Assyria and Babylon, the kingdom of the Medes and the Persians, the kingdom of the Chaldeans, and the kingdom of the Romans. God sent to each kingdom a craftsman to scatter it and humble it, and behold, the four kingdoms have completely vanished, their horns having been shattered, while the work of God remains successful, as the psalmist says: “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed… He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision” (Ps 2). These kingdoms were indicated by the four metals and the four great beasts which came up from the sea, one after another, in the vision of the prophet Daniel.

1.10.4.en: Second: Origen, St. Augustine, and many of the Fathers of the Church see that the number 4 refers to the four quarters of the world, that is, to the love of the world, and also refers to the body as being of the dust of this world. It is as though these horns that scatter “Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem” [19], “so that no man did lift up his head” [21], mean that the love of the world and the lusts of the body shatter Judah, that is, our union with the Lord Christ who came forth from the tribe of Judah, and shatter the new Israel, that is, our inner membership and the purity of our heart by which we see God. By them man does not lift up his head, but bows down his soul to be buried in the dust, as happened with the one who had the one talent (Mt 25:18); instead of rising with his body to heaven, his soul with the lusts of his body bows down to the earth.

1.10.5.en: Third: as Satan stirred up four horns against Jerusalem, God sent four craftsmen, as though God supports His children according to the extent that they enter into trials or afflictions; the more intense the warfare of Satan, the more help He sends. This is the work of God throughout the ages: since Pharaoh was violent, God sent Moses; since Ahab was wicked, God sent Elijah; and when Arius rose up against the Church, God prepared Athanasius the Apostolic; and so on. What goes on at the level of the Church of the Old Testament or of the New Testament is fulfilled every day in the life of each one of us.

1.10.6.en: Fourth: some of the Fathers see that the four horns are the warfare of the devil from every side, of which the Apostle Paul speaks: “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places” (Eph 6:12), and the Church has needed the four Gospels as the craftsmen who spoil the work of the devil with his four horns. Indeed Satan has used violent warfare with his four horns, but the Gospels have presented to us a new craft for overcoming Satan, which is the way of love and meekness; for the fire of the devil, with which he inflames the hearts of men against the believer, is overcome by love. As St. John Chrysostom says, fire is not put out by fire but by water; thus evil is not resisted by evil but by good.

1.10.7.en: And it is marvelous that, despite the meekness that characterized the four craftsmen, the horns trembled before them, just as Herod, the man of authority, feared before the unarmed St. John the Baptist (Mk 6:20), and as Felix the governor trembled before St. Paul the prisoner standing before him for trial (Acts 24:25)!
